scope.title: Eastern Europe, Russian/Soviet and Balkan source families
scope.sourceStrategy: National archives and constitutional treaties; occupation, federation and regime continuity require separate evidence.
scope.priorityRationale: Early source-family batches prioritise long snapshot presence, broad period potential and national archival/constitutional collections. Source availability is a planning expectation, not an entity-by-entity research finding. Families remain indivisible; no periods are researched now.

difficultCases.question: Source USSR appears in 1920 although the curated Union formation is dated 1922. Review civil-war source labels and republic/union relationships without inventing continuity.
Runtime mapping resolves outside the sourced existence interval. Review the source label and mapping before extending facts.

limitations: All new entities remain partial: editorial coverage limits are not complete lifetimes; unsupported offices, currencies, statistics, flags, seats and succession omitted.
Caucasian 1914 referents and later Soviet nesting are not assigned from raw names. First republican profiles cover only accepted institutions; Soviet phases remain gaps.
Ukraine 1920 has competing armed authorities. A generic source label does not independently identify the UPR or Soviet republic; mapping review retained.
USSR original undated mapping corrected to the existing sourced formation/dissolution bounds. 1920 remains unresolved; later enriched Union facts are unchanged.
Bulgaria’s narrow 1880 constitutional interval avoids suspension in 1881 and later royal elevation. Greek occupation/civil-war and Romanian postwar periods remain gaps.
Poland 1921/1926/1935 and Lithuania 1922/1927/1936 commencement details are not guessed; researched intervals leave explicit gaps.
Institutional summaries contain erroneous Greek 1922 republic-proclamation and Albanian 1937 invasion dates. These claims are excluded, not repeated as facts.
Montenegro’s treaty-only profile omits unsupported offices and later royal institutions. Dodecanese is Italian treaty title, not an independent state.
Russian civil-war source prerequisites stay unresolved/excluded; geometry and labels do not justify reclassification. No denominator change.

sources.title: Armenian parliamentary history
sources.usage: First Republic, cabinet accountability, parliamentary chairs and 2 December 1920 agreement. Later Soviet parliamentary forms are not projected backward.

sources.title: Armenia — diplomatic recognition history
sources.usage: 1918–1920 independence; US recognition 23 April 1920 without determining frontiers.

sources.title: History of the Azerbaijan parliamentary republic
sources.usage: Parliament opened 7 December 1918; formal chair Topchubashev; government in Baku from September 1918; republic ended April 1920. Partisan territorial interpretations are not adopted.

sources.title: Constitution of Georgia, 1921
sources.usage: Declaration 26 May 1918, March 1919 constituent elections, first constitution adopted 21 February 1921 during fighting. No projection into 1920.

sources.title: Fundamental Laws of the Russian Empire, 1906
sources.institution: Northern Virginia Community College / Robinson and Beard, Readings in Modern European History
sources.usage: Primary translated Articles 4, 7, 9, 17, 25, 86 establish imperial power, Duma and Council participation, ministers and hereditary throne.

sources.title: USSR: Sixty Years of Union — 1922 formation documents
sources.institution: Progress Publishers, Moscow, 1982; documents of the First Congress of Soviets
sources.usage: Primary resolution/declaration/treaty, printed pp. 161–168 (PDF pp. 159–166), dated 30 December 1922; formal federal institutions only. Ideological claims of voluntary unity are not adopted. Downloaded full document and read body.

sources.title: Treaty of Berlin, 13 July 1878, selected articles
sources.institution: Fordham University Internet Modern History Sourcebook
sources.usage: Primary Articles I, XXVI, XXXIV, XLIII: Bulgarian tributary principality and recognized independence of Montenegro, Serbia, Romania. Editorial modern geographic annotations are not used.

sources.title: Constitution of the Bulgarian Principality, 1879 — official 1887 edition
sources.institution: Bulgarian National Assembly / Ministry of Justice historical publication
sources.usage: Scanned body visually read PDF pp. 2–3, Articles 4–5, 9–12 and 18. Hereditary constitutional monarchy, Prince as head, representation and ministerial countersignature. Narrow 1880 coverage avoids later suspension.

sources.title: Constitutional history — 1864, 1927 and 1952 frameworks
sources.usage: Unicameral 1864 framework; confidence convention; 1927 republican bicameralism; 1952 crowned parliamentary framework. Erroneous 1922 republican proclamation chronology excluded.

sources.title: Short history of the parliamentary institution
sources.usage: 1866 bicameral constitution, 1923 constitutional monarchy, 10 February 1938 royal authoritarian government under Carol II. Adoption is not presumed commencement.

sources.title: History of Albanian parliamentarism
sources.institution: Albanian Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs
sources.usage: National Council legislative tenure 27 March–20 December 1920, 1928 royal/unicameral statute, 1946 parliament. Obvious incorrect 1937 invasion date excluded; no false Congress-convening date accepted.

sources.title: History of the Sejm
sources.usage: Small/March/April constitutional institutions, 1926 amendment, 1952 People’s Republic, and Krakow Senate/Representative Assembly. Full four-page body read.

sources.title: Assembly under the 1869 constitution
sources.usage: Documented assembly sessions and seats, distinct from later kingdom and constitutional changes. Local-calendar session dates not silently converted.

sources.title: Assembly under the 1903 constitution
sources.usage: Royal government; National Assembly sessions Belgrade then Niš in 1914, dated speaker records. Stop before wartime retreat; no inferred state succession.

sources.title: Constituent Assembly overview
sources.usage: Assembly 23 April 1919–20 December 1920, Tallinn legislative seat; July 1919 temporary constitution and 1920 adoption. Adoption not presumed commencement.

sources.title: Fourth Riigikogu overview
sources.usage: 1929–1932 legislative term, multiparty legislature and Karl Einbund’s parliamentary office, Tallinn sessions.

sources.title: Sixth Riigikogu overview
sources.usage: Bicameral legislature from 7 April 1938; emergency conditions, restricted parties, weak legislature, Päts elected president 24 April 1938.

sources.title: History of the legislature
sources.usage: Constituent Assembly, 1922–1934 Saeima and Kalniņš parliamentary office; coup 15 May 1934 transfers legislative power to Cabinet. No modern Riga address used as historical capital.

sources.title: Seimas elections 1920–1940
sources.usage: Constituent Seimas from 15 May 1920; 12 April 1927 dissolution and absence of elections until 1936; closure of other political parties. No inferred constitutional commencement dates.

sources.title: Lausanne Peace Treaty, League Treaty Series vol. 28, No. 701
sources.institution: League of Nations / United Nations Treaty Collection
sources.usage: Downloaded full original: p.13 ratification deposits August 1924, p.23 Article 15 Turkey renounces island rights to Italy. Post-1924 researched legal status; no invented local governor/seat.

sources.title: Historical city plans — Free City of Krakow
sources.institution: City of Krakow / Historical Museum collections
sources.usage: Congress of Vienna 1815 created Free, Independent and Strictly Neutral City of Krakow and surroundings; historical name Republic of Krakow.

sources.title: Final phase of the Ukrainian Revolution
sources.usage: Full HTML retrieved and body read: UPR army left Ukraine under Bolshevik pressure in November 1920. Evidence of competing armed authorities; generic map label not resolved by this institutional account. Advocacy language excluded.
